aiAgentFacts.fact: In 462 untreated hyperthyroid cats, median body weight at diagnosis was 4.36 kg versus a premorbid median of 5.45 kg recorded 1–2 years earlier (P<.0001).
Only 154 of 462 hyperthyroid cats (35.3%) were assessed as thin or emaciated, despite most having lost substantial weight from their own baseline.
Loss of muscle mass affected 357 of 462 hyperthyroid cats (77.3%) — more than twice the proportion that appeared underweight.
After treatment to a euthyroid state, median body weight rose from 4.1 kg to 5.0 kg, BCS from 3/5 to 3.5/5 and MCS from 2/3 to 3/3 (all P<.001) in the 117 cats reassessed.
Mild-to-moderate muscle wasting persisted in 45% of hyperthyroid cats after successful treatment.
Body condition score and muscle condition score are separate assessments; in this cohort the muscle findings were substantially worse than the body condition findings.
The study examined cats already diagnosed with hyperthyroidism and did not evaluate serial weight monitoring as a screening or early-detection method.
Weight loss and muscle loss are not specific to hyperthyroidism; this study did not compare against other causes of weight loss in older cats.

historyQuestions: Supported by the study's method rather than prescribed by it: retrieving a body weight recorded 1–2 years earlier is what makes current weight interpretable, since absolute weight alone concealed the loss in about two-thirds of these cats.
redFlags: Not defined by this study — no urgency thresholds or red-flag findings were evaluated.
differentialDiagnosesMentioned: Not addressed — the study characterises body composition within diagnosed hyperthyroid cats and does not evaluate competing causes of weight or muscle loss.
recommendedDiagnosticWorkups: The study's own assessments: body weight compared against a premorbid record, plus separate body condition and muscle condition scoring. Diagnosis of hyperthyroidism itself is laboratory-based and outside this study's scope.

limitations: Cross-sectional design on cats already diagnosed — provides no evidence that weight monitoring detects hyperthyroidism earlier
Premorbid weights were drawn from pre-existing clinical records rather than a standardised protocol, so measurement interval and conditions varied between cats
Only 117 of 462 cats (25%) were reassessed after treatment, and the follow-up window spanned 3–12 months
BCS and MCS are subjective clinical assessments; inter-observer variability was not reported in the abstract
No comparison group of non-hyperthyroid older cats, so the findings cannot distinguish hyperthyroid weight loss from weight loss due to other age-related disease
Weight and muscle loss are non-specific findings; this study supports no inference from weight change to a hyperthyroidism diagnosis
